specialists_or_stages: mantis-plan (Stage 4, run in-context: workspace/plan.json with six investigations I1-I6)
mantis-researcher (Stage 5, fanned out as six Wave-2 deep-audit sub-agents, one per top-level component)
mantis-dedupe (Stage 6, run in-context over the 46 returned findings)
mantis-review (Stage 7, run in-context: the 13 negative constraints applied as FP-01..FP-13)
mantis-critic (Stage 8, run in-context: production viability per finding)
mantis-calibrate (Stage 12, run in-context: severity assigned by the orchestrator)
architecture.fell_back_and_why: Ran in MODE-OFF, the pipeline's documented default: no --sync, so Startup Steps 1 and 3 (boundary sync, immutable snapshot pin) were skipped by contract, active_snapshot was left unwritten, and every stage read the live tree read-only. The target is a plain directory with no VCS metadata, so vcs_type resolved to none and the whole snapshot ladder was inapplicable. Researcher fan-out was capped at three concurrent sub-agents in two waves rather than the SKILL's suggested 10-20 Wave-1 plus 4-8 Wave-2, to respect the caller's budget ceiling; because the corpus is only 3,590 lines across 55 files, Wave 1 (rapid triage) was folded into Wave 2 and every file in every component was read in full, so the reduced fan-out cost no coverage. Stages 6, 7, 8, 12 and 14 were executed by the orchestrator in its own context instead of as separate sub-agents, for the same budget reason; the orchestrator independently re-read every cited line in the target before accepting a finding, which is the source-coherence check Stage 7 rule 12 requires. One environmental fallback: the chosen state directory workspace/findings/ already held 101 finding files from an unrelated earlier run against a different (AWS/TypeScript) target. Rather than delete another run's state, the foreign files were left untouched and this run's output was isolated by modification time; every finding below comes from a file written today and was independently re-verified against the target source.
architecture.budget_discipline: Three sub-agents in flight at a time, two waves, no stage waited on indefinitely. All six researchers returned, so the report is complete rather than partial.

stages_skipped: Stage 0 mantis-history - the target is a plain directory with no .git/.hg/.repo, so there is no VCS history to mine for past fixes; historical_learnings.jsonl would be empty.

Stage 0.5 mantis-structural-index - the workspace ships no helpers/query_structural_index.py and no catalog.sqlite could be built offline. The SKILL declares the index a HINT-only enhancement that degrades gracefully to grep, which is what was used.

Stage 1 mantis-summarize - directory mapping was folded into Stage 4 planning; at 55 files a per-directory mantis-summary.md would have cost more than it saved, and writing one into the target would have violated the read-only constraint.
Stage 2 and Stage 15.1 mantis-architecture - no persistent workspace/kb was carried between passes because this is a single-pass run; nothing downstream consumed the KB.
Stage 3 mantis-threat-model - the six investigations in plan.json carry the per-component trust boundaries directly, and the critic's KB-freshness gate is skipped in MODE-OFF by contract.

Stage 9 mantis-reproduce - no runtime available offline: no PHP, JVM, Airflow scheduler, Salt master, Flutter toolchain or MLflow server, and no container runtime to build one. Every finding is therefore static-analysis-confirmed rather than dynamically reproduced, and status reflects that. The single exception is the promptbridge eval() sandbox escape, which the I2 sub-agent executed locally in plain Python because the gadget needs no gateway.

Stage 10 mantis-chain - not run as its own stage; the two multi-step chains that matter are recorded inside the findings they span (blob traversal or XXE reaching the JWKS key and escalating to token forgery; deep link choosing the WebView URL that then receives the session token).
Stage 11 mantis-patch - the caller forbade modifying anything under the target, and patching requires writing to it. No patches generated, so no reattack loop.

Stage 13 mantis-reflect - this harness exposes no per-subagent transcript.jsonl path that the SKILL's Stage 13 could consume. Per the SKILL, an explicit empty list would be passed; with nothing to reflect over, the stage was skipped rather than run on fabricated inputs.
Stage 15 archive and pass increment - single-pass run; the state directory was shared with a foreign run, so archiving into it would have disturbed another run's data.

coverage.note: Every file in all six top-level directories was read in full by a researcher sub-agent, and every line cited in a finding was independently re-read by the orchestrator during Stage 7.

ruled_out.assertion: shell_exec in AdminController::logs is command injection
ruled_out.killed_by: No untrusted ingress reaches it. The only interpolated values are $unit from getenv('LOG_UNIT') (settings.php:38, process environment) and $lines, clamped by min(2000, max(10, (int) ...)) at line 83 and cast to int again at the sink.

ruled_out.assertion: ?sort=, ?dir= and ?limit= on GET /tickets are injectable alongside ?status=
ruled_out.killed_by: Sanitize::sortColumn does a strict in_array against the configured sortable list (Sanitize.php:28), direction collapses to ASC or DESC (line 33), and limit is int-cast and clamped. The mitigations work; only ?status= is unguarded.

ruled_out.assertion: Attachment upload is an unrestricted file upload leading to execution or stored XSS
ruled_out.killed_by: No extension or MIME allowlist exists, but Sanitize::filename strips traversal, files land in var/attachments outside the public docroot, and download serves them as application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment. No execution or rendering path exists in this tree.

ruled_out.assertion: Column-name injection through Db::update key names
ruled_out.killed_by: str_replace('`','',$col) turns a crafted key into an invalid identifier rather than injectable SQL. The real defect on that path is mass assignment (CWE-915), which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Committed database credentials in settings.php
ruled_out.killed_by: Every value is a getenv() lookup with a local-dev fallback; the fallbacks are a localhost DSN, the username support_app and an empty password. No real credential is committed.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the retrieval layer of the LLM gateway
ruled_out.killed_by: collection, query and slug are bound with %s placeholders and k is int()-cast. self.schema is f-string interpolated but comes from config, not from the request, so no attacker-controlled value reaches the interpolation.

ruled_out.assertion: sql_console raw string concatenation is an exploitable SQL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: Traced rather than dismissed for looking like dead code: it is absent from registry() at tools.py:80-85, sql_console is false in config.yaml:37, and the dispatcher can only call names present in the enabled registry. No request path reaches it.

ruled_out.assertion: yaml.safe_load of the gateway config is unsafe deserialization
ruled_out.killed_by: safe_load is the safe API and the config path is __file__-relative, not attacker-influenced.

ruled_out.assertion: TokenVerifier.verifyLegacy accepts unsigned JWTs, so authentication can be bypassed
ruled_out.killed_by: parseUnsecuredClaims is genuinely dangerous, but a corpus-wide grep for verifyLegacy and legacyEnabled returns only their own definitions. handle() calls verify() only, and legacyTokens is false in config.json:27. No ingress exists. Recorded as a latent landmine one call site away from being critical.

ruled_out.assertion: The main JWT verification path is flawed (alg confusion, missing exp/aud, .equals HMAC compare)
ruled_out.killed_by: verify() uses jjwt 0.12.5 parseSignedClaims with verifyWith(SecretKey), requireIssuer and requireAudience; that API rejects unsigned tokens and enforces exp by default. No string comparison of a MAC anywhere. The mitigation works.

ruled_out.assertion: listByOwner's dynamic ORDER BY is injectable like searchByTag
ruled_out.killed_by: The sort column is a SortColumn enum with hardcoded strings whose parse() falls back to CREATED_AT for unknown input, and limit is %d on an int. searchByTag is the outlier, not the house pattern.

ruled_out.assertion: RetentionSweeper's concatenated SELECT is SQL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: bucket and keepDays come only from the config block (config.json:18-22), keepDays is typed int, and MetadataRepository.insert - the only writer of blob_key - has no caller in the corpus. No request path feeds the sweeper.

ruled_out.assertion: Known-vulnerable pinned dependencies in pom.xml
ruled_out.killed_by: Could not be substantiated offline. vertx 4.5.7, jjwt 0.12.5 and flyway 10.13.0 could not be checked against an advisory feed in this environment, and inventing a CVE id would violate the source-coherence rule. Recorded as unassessed, not as clean.

ruled_out.assertion: Pillar top.sls '*' glob leaks each minion's secrets to the whole fleet
ruled_out.killed_by: Pillar renders per minion, so each minion only ever receives its own agent_token. The remaining keys are infrastructure descriptors, not secrets.

ruled_out.assertion: Grain-based targeting lets a rogue minion escalate by self-assigning roles
ruled_out.killed_by: Grains are minion-controlled, but both pillar branches serve the same fleet sls and the states a rogue minion would gain write only that minion's own token and install its own package. No cross-minion privilege gain to point at.

ruled_out.assertion: proxy_pass SSRF through a minion-influenced upstream in the nginx template
ruled_out.killed_by: upstream_host and upstream_port are static master-side pillar values (pillar/fleet.sls:26-27). No grain or minion input reaches the upstream block.

ruled_out.assertion: Access-Control-Allow-Origin '*' on /assets/ is a CORS misconfiguration
ruled_out.killed_by: The location serves cookieless static files from /srv/www with no credentials allowed, which is the correct use of '*'. The credentialed block at lines 37-38 uses a single fixed master-side origin.

ruled_out.assertion: The committed CI deploy key is an exposed secret
ruled_out.killed_by: It is an ssh-ed25519 public key consumed by ssh_auth.present. Committing a public key is not secret exposure.

ruled_out.assertion: sql/upsert_ledger.sql is injectable through Airflow template rendering
ruled_out.killed_by: The %(partition)s markers are real psycopg2 pyformat bind placeholders, not Jinja. The file is also unreferenced - the operator builds its own f-string instead, which is the substance of the reported CWE-89.

ruled_out.assertion: archive_report's subprocess with shell=True is command injection
ruled_out.killed_by: Every argv element passes through shlex.quote at line 75 and dest_prefix is alphanumeric- and length-checked at reconcile.py:34-38. The mitigation works.

ruled_out.assertion: LedgerExportOperator prefix reaches os.path.join and traverses
ruled_out.killed_by: validate_conf at reconcile.py:37 rejects anything non-alphanumeric after stripping hyphen and underscore, so no slash or dot-dot survives, and export runs only downstream of that gate. Fragile wiring, but not exploitable as configured.

ruled_out.assertion: pickle.load in the transforms cache is unsafe deserialization
ruled_out.killed_by: grep for read_cache and write_cache returns only their definitions; nothing in the component calls either, and _cache_path strips everything outside [a-z0-9_]. No ingress.

ruled_out.assertion: SANDBOX_BASIC_AUTH is a committed credential
ruled_out.killed_by: A published demo pair for a nightly-wiped sandbox tenant carrying generated rows. Reporting it would be a false positive.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the delivery detail screen's local query
ruled_out.killed_by: deliveryId is typed int at line 19 and the only ingress parses it with int.tryParse and returns on null (main.dart:42-43). Interpolating an int carries no injectable text.

ruled_out.assertion: Open redirect through the deep link's next parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: followNext enforces an exact-match _trustedHosts.contains(target.host) at line 34, and userinfo tricks resolve host to the attacker domain and are blocked. The guard works - which is what makes its absence on proofUrl a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The App Links host filter is missing android:autoVerify
ruled_out.killed_by: autoVerify="true" is present on the https filter at line 40. The assertion is contradicted by the file.

ruled_out.assertion: The map tile key in the Flutter client is a leaked credential
ruled_out.killed_by: pk.map-tiles-public-demo-0000 is a publishable tile key scoped to tile endpoints and present in the vendor's own public demo. Not a secret.

ruled_out.assertion: Exported Android components expose sensitive functionality
ruled_out.killed_by: MainActivity's exported=true is mandatory for a LAUNCHER activity, RouteTrackingService is exported=false at line 50, and no receivers or providers are declared. Only the intent filter's content matters, and that is folded into the deep-link finding.

findings.title: Entire /admin route group is registered without AuthMiddleware
findings.evidence: index.php:47-55 registers the /tickets group and terminates it with `->add(new AuthMiddleware($pdo))`. The /admin group at lines 58-63 registers /tenants, /sessions, /logs and POST /impersonate and closes at line 63 with no `->add(...)` at all. The only stated control is the comment on line 57, 'The console is only published on the internal VLAN', which is prose, not a control in this tree.
findings.impact: Any client that can reach the listening port reads every tenant record and every live session row, and can POST /admin/impersonate to mint a valid session token for an arbitrary user id. Full unauthenticated takeover of the API.
findings.recommendation: Attach `->add(new AuthMiddleware($pdo))` to the /admin group exactly as the /tickets group does, and add a role check on top of it.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress is the unauthenticated HTTP request itself; no data-flow tracing is needed because the missing control is on the route, not on a value.
This is absent authentication on a privileged route group, not a missing header or a defence-in-depth nicety.
Searched for a compensating mitigation and found only a comment; a deployment claim in a code comment is not an enforced control.

scope.established_by: Slim route registration in public/index.php: middleware binds per group via ->add(), and the /admin group closes without one.
scope.narrowed_by: Reachability depends on the listener being exposed; the tree ships no proxy or firewall config that would confine it.

searched.for: any global $app->add() that would cover all groups
searched.found: only the CORS middleware at line 25 and the error middleware at line 39; neither authenticates

searched.for: a role or session check inside the handlers
searched.found: nothing - grep for 'role' returns only docblock text, no authorization code

searched.for: a reverse-proxy or firewall config enforcing the claimed VLAN restriction
searched.found: nothing

findings.title: POST /admin/impersonate mints a session token for any user id with no authorization check
findings.evidence: impersonate() reads `$body['user_id']` (line 58), looks the user up, then INSERTs a fresh row into api_sessions with that user's id and tenant_id and returns the cleartext secret to the caller (lines 66-74). There is no check of the caller's role, tenant, or identity anywhere in the method or the class.
findings.impact: Privilege escalation to any account in any tenant. Combined with the missing group middleware it is anonymous; even with authentication restored, any low-privilege caller could still escalate to an administrator.
findings.recommendation: Require an authenticated administrator, verify the caller's role, confine the target to the caller's tenant, and write an audit event for every impersonation.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress cited at AdminController.php:58, the parsed request body; the value flows to the session INSERT at line 72.
This is not a hypothetical caller misusing a safe function - the handler itself performs the privileged act with no check.
Absent authorization on a session-minting endpoint is a primary control, not hygiene.

scope.established_by: The handler body itself: it accepts a caller-supplied user_id and issues credentials for it.
scope.narrowed_by: Distinct from the route-level finding: this defect survives adding AuthMiddleware, because the middleware authenticates but never authorizes.

searched.for: any role/permission gate in the class
searched.found: nothing - no reference to the 'role' request attribute that AuthMiddleware sets at line 64

searched.for: whether the middleware performs authorization as well as authentication
searched.found: it sets user_id, tenant_id and role attributes but enforces no role anywhere

findings.title: SQL injection in GET /tickets via the ?status= filter concatenated by Sanitize::statusClause
findings.evidence: statusClause() splits the caller's string on commas and pastes the parts straight between single quotes: `return " AND status IN ('" . implode("','", $parts) . "')";`. Nothing escapes a quote. TicketController::index reads `$q['status']` from the query string and appends the result to the statement at line 35, which is then executed by Db::all with only the tenant id bound.
findings.impact: Reads any table the application user can reach, across every tenant, from an authenticated low-privilege session; the injected text lands in the WHERE clause of a SELECT, so UNION-based extraction works directly.
findings.recommendation: Bind the status values as placeholders - build `IN (?,?,?)` from the count of parts and pass the parts as parameters - or validate each part against the enumerated status set.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress at TicketController.php:35, `$q['status']` from getQueryParams(); sink is the concatenation at Sanitize.php:47 executed at TicketController.php:40.
The surrounding code does use bound parameters for the tenant id, which is precisely why this hand-built fragment stands out; the flaw is not an absence of paranoia but an unparameterised value.
code_paths narrowed to the helper that builds the fragment plus its single injecting caller.

scope.established_by: The concatenation in Sanitize::statusClause, reached from the ?status= query parameter.
scope.narrowed_by: The sibling parameters on the same endpoint are safe: ?sort= is allowlisted and ?dir=/?limit= are normalised, so only ?status= is injectable.

searched.for: an escaping or allowlist step applied to the status parts
searched.found: nothing - array_filter/trim only remove empties and whitespace

searched.for: whether the caller validates status before calling the helper
searched.found: nothing - the raw query value is cast to string and passed straight in at line 35

searched.for: whether Db::all re-parses or escapes the SQL string
searched.found: no - it prepares the already-concatenated string and binds only the explicit parameter array

findings.title: Path traversal to arbitrary file read in the attachment download route
findings.evidence: download() builds `$path = $base . '/' . rawurldecode((string) $args['name']);`. The route is declared `/tickets/{id}/attachments/{name:.+}` (index.php:53), so `{name}` matches slashes, and rawurldecode() turns %2e%2e%2f back into ../. The upload path sanitises names with Sanitize::filename, but the download path does not, and the file is then read with file_get_contents and returned in the body.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user reads any file the PHP process can open - configuration, credentials, application source, /etc/passwd - by requesting a crafted attachment name.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the joined path with realpath() and reject anything that does not remain inside the attachments directory; also run the name through Sanitize::filename on the read path as the upload path already does.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress at AttachmentController.php:53, the {name} route argument; sink is the file_get_contents at line 59.
Looked for the mitigation that exists on upload and confirmed it is simply not applied on download.
Directly and repeatably triggerable with one crafted request; no timing or environmental precondition.

scope.established_by: String concatenation of a URL-decoded, slash-permitting route argument into a filesystem path.
scope.narrowed_by: The ticket id segment is cast to int and cannot traverse; only the {name} segment carries the flaw.

searched.for: whether filename() is applied on the read path
searched.found: it exists and strips traversal, but download() never calls it - only upload() at line 41 does

searched.for: a realpath/containment check after joining
searched.found: nothing - the only gate is is_file() at line 55, which a traversed path satisfies

findings.title: GET /tickets/{id} returns any tenant's ticket and its comments with no ownership check
findings.evidence: show() selects `FROM tickets WHERE id = ?` binding only the path id. The tenant attribute that AuthMiddleware puts on the request is never consulted. The same class demonstrates the correct pattern 54 lines later: update() at line 106 selects `WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?` before it will touch a row.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant disclosure of every ticket body and comment thread in the database by enumerating integer ids from any authenticated account.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND tenant_id = ?` to the show() lookup and to the comments query, binding the tenant attribute, exactly as update() already does.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress at TicketController.php:49, the {id} route argument; the missing constraint is on the query at line 52.
No caller misuse is required - the handler itself omits the tenant predicate.
The construct is on a production controller, not a test or sample path.

scope.established_by: The tenant predicate is absent from the read query in show(), while the request already carries an authenticated tenant_id attribute.
scope.narrowed_by: update() on the same resource is correctly scoped, so the exposure is read-only through this handler.

searched.for: a tenant filter anywhere in show()
searched.found: nothing - the only bound parameter is the id

searched.for: whether tenant scoping is enforced centrally in middleware
searched.found: no - the middleware only attaches tenant_id as a request attribute; enforcing it is left to each handler

findings.title: Attachment endpoints never check that the ticket belongs to the caller's tenant
findings.evidence: All three attachment handlers derive their storage directory from `(int) $args['id']` alone. The controller is constructed with only `$settings` (it has no PDO handle at all), so it cannot check ticket ownership even in principle, and it does not read the tenant_id request attribute anywhere.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant read, write and delete of attachment files: an authenticated user of tenant A uploads into, downloads from and deletes another tenant's ticket attachment directory by supplying that ticket's id.
findings.recommendation: Pass the PDO handle into the controller and gate every handler on a `SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?` lookup before touching the filesystem.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress at AttachmentController.php:52, the {id} route argument, used directly as the directory component.
Primary location set to the shared directory derivation; the three handlers that repeat it are listed in scope.
This is a distinct missing control from the traversal finding on the same file, not an invented adjacent class - the traversal is in {name}, this is in {id}.

scope.established_by: Every attachment handler maps the ticket id straight to a directory without an ownership lookup.
scope.narrowed_by: The AuthMiddleware still requires a valid session, so the attacker must hold some account; it need not be in the target tenant.

searched.for: an ownership query or tenant attribute read
searched.found: nothing - the class holds no database handle at all

searched.for: whether the router scopes attachment routes differently from ticket routes
searched.found: no - they sit in the same /tickets group behind the same middleware

findings.title: Mass assignment in PATCH /tickets/{id}: the configured fillable allowlist is never read
findings.class: mass assignment / improperly controlled modification of object attributes
findings.evidence: update() takes the whole parsed body as `$changes` (line 113), unsets only `id` and `created_at`, and hands the remainder to Db::update, which builds a SET clause from whatever keys survive. settings.php:32 defines `'fillable' => ['subject', 'body', 'priority']`, and a repository-wide grep for 'fillable' returns only that definition - no code ever reads it.
findings.impact: A requester rewrites columns that are not theirs to set: `status`, `assignee_id`, `requester_id` and, most seriously, `tenant_id`, which moves a ticket into another tenant or pulls another tenant's ticket into their own view.
findings.recommendation: Intersect the submitted keys with `$this->settings['tickets']['fillable']` before calling Db::update, and reject rather than silently drop unexpected keys.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress at TicketController.php:113, getParsedBody(); sink is the dynamic SET clause built in Db::update at Db.php:68-74.
An unenforced allowlist that the configuration explicitly declares is a broken control, not a missing nicety.
Checked whether Db::update's backtick stripping mitigates it: it prevents identifier injection but does nothing about which columns may be written.

scope.established_by: The gap between the declared fillable list in settings.php and the update path that never consults it.
scope.narrowed_by: The handler does verify ticket ownership at line 106, so the attacker must own the ticket being modified - which is enough to move it into another tenant.

searched.for: any reader of the 'fillable' setting
searched.found: nothing - grep across the component returns only the definition at settings.php:32

searched.for: whether Db::update restricts column names
searched.found: it strips backticks at lines 68 and 74, which blocks identifier injection but permits any real column

findings.title: CORS reflects the caller's Origin while allowing credentials
findings.evidence: The middleware computes `$allow = ($configured === '*' && $origin !== '') ? $origin : $configured;` and emits it as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. settings.php ships `allow_origin => '*'` and `allow_credentials => true`, so the reflected branch is the default. Reflecting the origin is what makes the credentialed combination effective, since a literal '*' would be rejected by browsers when credentials are allowed.
findings.impact: Any web page a signed-in user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the API and read the responses, exfiltrating that user's tickets and, together with the mass-assignment finding, rewriting their tenant_id.
findings.recommendation: Replace reflection with an explicit allowlist of partner origins checked against the Origin header, and only then emit Allow-Credentials.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress is the attacker-chosen Origin request header read at index.php:29; it is echoed into the response header at line 33.
This is not a missing header - it is a present header computed from attacker input in a way that grants access.
Reproducible with a static attacker page; requires a victim with a live session, which is why it is rated medium rather than high.

scope.established_by: The reflection branch in the CORS middleware combined with the shipped '*' and credentials-true configuration.
scope.narrowed_by: Exploitation needs a victim who is authenticated and visits attacker-controlled content, so it is not directly reachable by an unauthenticated attacker alone.

searched.for: whether a fixed origin is configured by default
searched.found: no - allow_origin is '*' and allow_credentials is true

searched.for: an Origin allowlist or Vary: Origin handling
searched.found: nothing - the value is echoed unconditionally when configured is '*'

findings.title: Session token digest compared with loose, non-constant-time !=
findings.evidence: After looking the session up by the 8-character token prefix, the middleware confirms the secret with `if ($session['token_digest'] != $digest)`. Two hex digests are compared with PHP's loose operator and with a short-circuiting byte comparison rather than hash_equals().
findings.impact: The comparison leaks timing information about how many leading bytes of the digest matched, and PHP's numeric-string juggling makes two digests of the form 0e[0-9]+ compare equal. Both are real defects, but the stored digest would itself have to fall into that shape for the juggling path, and the prefix lookup narrows the timing oracle sharply, so practical exploitation is remote.
findings.recommendation: Use `hash_equals($session['token_digest'], $digest)`, which is both strict and constant-time.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress is the attacker-supplied bearer token read earlier in the middleware; it reaches the comparison as $digest at line 43.
The code does use a secure standard hash, so this is not linting the hash choice - the defect is the comparison operator on a secret.

Strict reproducibility is doubtful: the timing signal is small behind a database round trip and the type-juggling path needs the stored digest to have a specific shape. This is why the severity is low rather than medium.

scope.established_by: The single equality check that confirms the full session secret.
scope.narrowed_by: The prefix lookup at line 51 means an attacker cannot iterate the digest freely; only the final confirmation is weakly compared.

searched.for: a hash_equals or === comparison elsewhere on the path
searched.found: nothing - line 58 is the only secret comparison

searched.for: how digests are produced, to confirm both sides are hex sha256
searched.found: hash('sha256', $secret) at line 72, so both sides are 64-char hex

findings.title: Legacy search controller concatenates ?q= into SQL and is retained in the tree
findings.evidence: The controller builds its statement by concatenating the q query parameter directly into a LIKE clause. A repository-wide grep for 'LegacySearch' returns only the class definition itself - no route registers it and nothing instantiates it, so today it is unreachable.
findings.impact: No exposure while it stays unwired. The moment anyone registers the route - which is the obvious reason to keep the file - it becomes a direct injection point equivalent to the ?status= finding.

findings.class: use of a one-way hash with a predictable salt
findings.evidence: The key is `sha256.convert(utf8.encode('$_keySalt:$installationId'))` where _keySalt is the compile-time constant 'courier-app-v3' at line 17 and installationId is documented at line 15 as the stable per-installation identifier generated at first launch. Neither input is a secret, and a single unsalted SHA-256 pass is not a key-derivation function.
findings.impact: Anyone who learns the installation id - it is not treated as a secret and travels with telemetry and support flows - reconstructs the key offline in one hash operation and decrypts everything SecureBox sealed, including the stored PIN.
findings.recommendation: Derive the key from a random value held in the platform keystore, or from a user secret through a real KDF (Argon2id or PBKDF2 with a per-install random salt and a high iteration count).

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress is knowledge of the installation id plus access to the ciphertext; both are obtainable by an attacker with device or backup access.
SHA-256 is a sound hash, but using it as a KDF over two non-secret inputs is a key-management defect, not a demand for extra paranoia.
Given the id and the ciphertext the derivation is deterministic and instant.

scope.established_by: The key derivation expression used by every seal and open call in the class.
scope.narrowed_by: The sealed PIN itself sits behind flutter_secure_storage, so an attacker must first defeat the Keystore to obtain the ciphertext - which is why this is medium rather than high.

searched.for: a random or keystore-backed key source
searched.found: nothing - the key is always recomputed from the salt and installation id

searched.for: where the sealed value is stored, to judge how reachable the ciphertext is
searched.found: flutter_secure_storage at line 46, which raises the bar and bounds the severity

findings.title: AES-CBC values are sealed with a fixed all-zero IV
findings.class: generation of predictable IV with CBC mode
findings.evidence: `static final enc.IV _iv = enc.IV.fromLength(16);` produces sixteen zero bytes, and the comment above it states the IV is fixed so a value sealed by one build can still be opened by the next. seal() and open() both use that constant IV with AES in CBC mode.
findings.impact: Identical plaintexts under the same key produce identical ciphertexts, so an observer can tell when a sealed value is unchanged or matches a known candidate, and CBC's first block loses its semantic security. It is a real cryptographic defect but does not by itself recover plaintext.
findings.recommendation: Generate a random IV per seal and store it alongside the ciphertext - the upgrade-compatibility concern the comment raises is solved by prefixing the IV to the output, not by fixing it.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Not a data-flow finding; the defect is the constant IV in the construction itself.
A fixed IV under CBC is a documented misuse of the primitive rather than a stylistic complaint.
Exploiting it requires the attacker to already hold ciphertexts and a plaintext candidate, and the stronger key-derivation defect in the same file dominates. That is why it is low.

scope.established_by: The shared constant IV used by the seal path.
scope.narrowed_by: Bounded by the same secure-storage barrier as the key-derivation finding, and its impact is inference rather than decryption.

searched.for: a per-value random IV anywhere in the class
searched.found: nothing - _iv is a single static final

searched.for: the cipher mode, to confirm the IV actually matters
searched.found: AESMode.cbc at line 29, where a repeated IV is a genuine weakness

findings.title: Full API response bodies containing recipient PII are written to the device log
findings.class: insertion of sensitive information into log file
findings.evidence: The client logs the complete response body for each request. Delivery responses carry recipient names, addresses and contact details.
findings.impact: Recipient personal data accumulates in the device log. On modern Android another app cannot read it, so realising this needs adb access, a device-log collector, or a crash-reporting SDK that ships logs off-device.
findings.recommendation: Log only the status code and a request identifier, and gate any body logging behind a debug-only build flag.

triage.reason: Line verified by direct read of the file during the review stage; path, symbol and line all exist as cited.
Ingress is the server response; it reaches the log sink at client.dart:66.

This sits close to the missing-hygiene rule - on a current Android release the log is not readable across apps. It is reported at low severity for that reason rather than dropped, because the data is personal data of third parties rather than of the app's own user.
Not a resource-exhaustion claim.

scope.established_by: The response logging call on the shared client path, so it applies to every endpoint.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires local log access; not remotely reachable.

searched.for: a kDebugMode guard or redaction on the log call
searched.found: nothing - it logs unconditionally
